I asked Secretary Duffy what Americans should be able to do, if we get this decade right, that they can't do today.

Sean Duffy is the Secretary of Transportation, and he sat down with me at our Startup Industrial Base event in DC today. He went straight to how our country's air traffic gets managed.

At the command center, people sit in front of six screens with a paper flight chart above them, trying to make the calls on weather and routing.

His example: four planes reach the same runway at the same time and only one can land. See it two hours out, speed up two, slow one down, and each one lands when the runway is open. "Like, not complicated stuff, but we don't do any of this."

Paper and pencil and minimal human augmentation from software looks like this: Say an airport can take 15 planes in a 15 minute window. "Well, the airlines will schedule 32." He says he's handing the airlines that data and asking them to spread out.

The tool is SMART, from Air Space Intelligence, a small company he says competed with the biggest companies and won. It predicts. His stage example: a 2.5 hour ground stop might only need 45 minutes. He's taken heat for supposedly handing air traffic control to AI. Duffy's answer? "it's dumb AI, not smart AI." Controllers still make every call.

None of this needs a breakthrough. It needs the will of the people to know they need to use software and be ok with AI augmentation instead of insisting on a paper chart and copper wire.

The Pentagon's 300-page RFP "was designed for a lawyer and a lobbyist and a prime contractor to know how to fill out."

That's Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research & Engineering, saying it out loud to a room full of founders at our Startup Industrial Base event in DC today.

A 10-person startup reads 300 pages, gets one thing wrong, gets kicked out. Or survives and grinds through 3, 6, 9, 12 month rounds until it's two years in. Meanwhile the prime has a team whose whole job is filling out every page perfectly.

Emil’s fix? Write a one pager not 300. "I need to fly a missile 500 miles in this kind of environment." If your payload won't work, you hear that fast. Target is 90 days.

Drone Dominance runs the same way. Apply, top 20 go to a fly-off, objective metrics, cuts every round, and he says half a billion dollars of orders at the end. "I'd rather know if I lose and why." Miss round one and there are more rounds coming, and "it'll be 2 or 3" winners, not one.

Cost per intercept is the game now. Shoot down a $50k drone with a Patriot missile and "the math doesn't math." He's funding directed energy and high power microwave that cost thousands, not millions.

The tech was never what kept startups out. The 300 pages were. Two pages and a fly-off means the best product can actually win, and the prime has to compete like everyone else.

This is interesting work to think about the long-run case. I am trying to wrap my head around how possible this is in practice outside of just a steady-state environment.

The ~5x wage increase comes with an ~8x rise in output per worker and a gross savings rate going from ~20% to ~40% (?) of output if I have that right? The wage gain therefore then seems to be mostly produced by the productivity event.

Over the last two decades while capital share has risen materially, labor productivity growth has sat constant at 1.5–2%. Does that discredit this analysis by implying a loss in bargaining power for labor or some other driving force rather than a technological revolution?

Another question I'd be curious your views on is that I believe this assumes capital and labor remain complements? If AI actually starts to replace workers and increases the elasticity of substitution, would it then threaten the rise in labor's productivity/compensation?

In politics I guess the transitional dynamics you mention are sometimes the most important part as that starts to bring a multitude of other factors into the environment (eg immigration and work force demographics).

having used Tesla FSD for a while and taken a representative sample of Waymos, my conclusion is.... 

FSD feels much smoother, more natural, and human-like. It's an overall more enjoyable ride and I don't get carsick from sudden braking/acceleration. (note: i've only ever used the latest edition of FSD) 

Waymo is MUCH more risk averse, more jittery, and nervous. It kind of feels like a student driver white knuckling their first ever car ride. It is scared of its own shadow and brakes sharply all the time if it thinks something weird might be going on. 

This may be due to the fact that the model _has_ to be more risk averse fundamentally since there is no backup driver. Waymo also gets stuck in weird failure modes. Yesterday we looped around in a random parking lot for 10 minutes because it couldn't figure out which exit it liked better. You feel weirdly helpless in those situations... like there should be a way to tell the car "hey little buddy I know youre scared, but it's actually totally fine. you can go this way it's ok." In complex situations it tends to freeze; but defaulting to inaction isn't always the right move. It often also takes a lot longer to arrive than it says it will; I assume because it's going endlessly round a roundabout or stuck in some other weird glitch. Still better than a human Uber driver though; at least with Waymo you know that it will eventually arrive. 

Waymo also hates picking you up where you want to be picked up and will insist on going to some parking lot two blocks away. 

Either way after a week taking Waymos in the bay area I actually gave up and went back to human Uber drivers and felt relieved. The newer Waymo vehicles also feel junkier than the Jaguars. 

On the margin, I still probably prefer a Waymo to a human driver, but I think the model has a loooong way to go.

tweets.text:
Micron Q4: five takeaways

1) Korea called it, again. Three weeks ago the first-ten-day export data set a record while everyone was busy calling the peak in AI. Micron just printed $54.2bn of revenue, +379% year-on-year, beat consensus by $3bn, and guided the next quarter to $61.5bn against a street at $57bn. And note that Q4 was a 14-week quarter, so the Q1 guide on a normal 13-week quarter is an even bigger sequential step than the headline suggests. The earnings cycle is not slowing. It is accelerating into a market that has spent the summer compressing multiples.

2) The cyclicality debate is over, for now. This is the argument we have had for many months: is memory still a boom-bust commodity? Gross margin at 87% and roughly $100bn of remaining performance obligations across the strategic customer agreements say the business has changed. Contracts do not remove the cycle, they stretch it. And $33bn of free cash flow in the quarter, $73bn of cash on the balance sheet: they fund the Idaho buildout and return the excess without touching the debt markets. That is the one thing the neoclouds cannot say.

3) Valuation is still absurd. On the new Q1 guide, run-rate EPS is about $153. At $1,070 that is roughly 7x. The S&P is on 22x. CrowdStrike is near 200x. The market is still pricing memory profits as if they end next year; the guidance says they rise into 2027, when HBM4 volume lands. Way, way too cheap remains the verdict.

4) It confirms the book. Quality of earnings is the factor in a hiking cycle, and Micron is the definition of it. Memory is the all-weather asset in the frontier-slows debate: training wants bandwidth, inference wants capacity, and both showed up in this print. US memory over Korea into the licence decision. We hold. We do not add after a 290% run.

5) The number to watch is capex. FY26 capex was $27bn against $62bn of free cash flow. If all three memory makers raise capex sharply at once, that is the first 2027-28 warning sign. Management already flagged that the rate of price increases is moderating, which means volume and contracts are now doing the work rather than price. That is exactly what you want if you own it for durability rather than for the spike. We do.

1: Give the firm experience

I would utilise the research around creating a memory enhanced trading agent.

every investment/trade I give to my agent would become an experience.

what did we think would happen? what actually happened? what did we get wrong?

next time we find a similar investment, retrieve it and learn from it.

remembering everything is useless if you don’t know which memories are actually valuable.

the agent wouldn’t just have memory, it would learn which memories are useful.

markets change constantly.

revenue guidance changes. tokenomics change. valuations change. narratives change.

I would use validity-aware memory so my agents know when information is outdated, updated or completely wrong.

this is where it gets ridiculous.

if my crypto agent misses a major token unlock I don’t just want it to remember:

“i missed the token unlock”

I want the mistake to change how it researches every future token.

mistake = a lesson = a new research rule = a new test to improve the agent.

having 5 agents agreeing with each other is pointless if they’re basically the same agent 5 times.

finally I would build my own benchmark.

every time I change the system I want to know:

> did research accuracy improve?
> did it miss less important information?
> did it make fewer unsupported claims?
> did it actually make better decisions?

combine all six and you don’t really have an AI trading bot anymore.

you have a damn hedge fund that can remember, learn from its mistakes and hopefully get better the longer you use it.

When do you sell a stock? $WGS 

$WGS was trading around $80 when it reported earnings. The company said its average reimbursement per test was lower than expected as more patients shifted to whole genome testing.

The stock collapsed. I thought the market was treating this as a permanent problem. Whole genome testing gives you a more complete picture, yet insurers were reimbursing it at a lower rate than exome testing. I believed that gap could improve as coverage became more established.

When WGS fell below $40, I recommended backing up the truck. I put 30% of my own portfolio into it.

Slowly, the stock started climbing back toward $80. But as it moved from $80 toward $100, the story changed. At the lower price, we were assuming reimbursement would improve. At the higher price, the market was already beginning to price that improvement in. And full reimbursement for everything GeneDx is doing still wasn’t there. The stock may have run ahead of itself.

So, when do you sell? I don’t give people a sell price. If you have a five-year view, a 20% drop may not change the thesis. If you have a shorter timeline and the stock is up 140%, you may decide to take some profits. That’s up to you. I’ll explain why I buy a stock, but I’ll never tell you when to sell it because each person has a different time frame.

While it isn't all about the quid pro quo between the company and the employee, this balance must be economically viable for the relationships to be sustainable. 

Set policies that clearly define this quid pro quo, and be measured, but not excessively precise, when shifting it around. While you should by and large stick to the arrangement, you should also recognize that there are rare, special times when employees will need a bit of extra time off and there are times that the company will require employees to give it extra hours. The company should pay for above-normal work one way or another, and employees should be docked for below-normal work. 

The give-and-take should roughly equal out over time. #principleoftheday

When software becomes a commodity, the moat is how much value you deliver per unit of compute.

Anyone can build the same features. Few can serve as many users, across as many use cases, without restrictive limits.

Model quality compounds that advantage: better results with less compute mean higher gross margins and more compute to train the next, more efficient model.

That’s the winning flywheel for the next 24 months.
